messages.content: You are the neutral rapporteur of a technology readiness review panel. Consolidate, attribute and preserve disagreement; do not decide and do not add technical claims of your own.

# Synthesis: assess · T25

## Claude Opus 5.5


# TRL assessment: T25, target-local and SEL1 cargo-node navigation and control

## Scope and assumptions

The requirement is mostly TBD, so I fixed working values from the revised architecture. Each one is open to challenge.

| Parameter | Working value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Payload per transfer | 150–300 t | Architecture |
| Stack mass at the node (payload + tug + residual propellant) | ~200–450 t | Assumes tug dry mass 10–75 t at 10–30 kg/kWe. This is my estimate, not project data. |
| Array power and area | 1–2.5 MWe. Roughly 3,000 m² (1 MWe at 1 AU) up to ~12,000 m² (2.5 MWe at 1.3 AU), at ~200–330 W/m² | My calculation |
| EP thrust and acceleration | ~35–170 N, giving ~7×10⁻⁵ to 7×10⁻⁴ m/s² | Thrust = 2ηP/(g₀·Isp) with η = 0.5–0.65 at 2,000–3,000 s |
| Traffic per node | ~2–17 arrivals/yr | 0.6–2.5 kt/yr ÷ 150–300 t, consistent with 10–18 tugs on 1.5–5 yr round trips |
| Lifetime traffic | ~30–180 proximity campaigns per node over 10–15 yr | Derived from the line above |
| Light time | SEL1 ~5 s one-way. NEA at 0.9–1.3 AU heliocentric gives up to ~20 min one-way, plus solar-conjunction outages. | Geometry |

**What T25 includes:**
- relative navigation;
- proximity guidance, navigation and control (GNC) of the massive, flexible stack;
- stationkeeping and hovering;
- collision avoidance, including against the site's own debris;
- capture, contact, mate and separation dynamics for payload hand-off.

**What T25 excludes:**
- lifting product from the NEA surface to the tug;
- the propulsion string (EP thrusters and power).

### Errors in the related RQs that this rating does not inherit

- **rq-0-17 acceleration.** It sizes attachment loads at 0.01–0.1 m/s². The stated power and Isp give ~10⁻⁴ m/s², which is 15–1,500× lower. Sustained cargo loads under EP are therefore tens of newtons, not 2–20 kN. The design-driving loads are contact and RCS transients, not thrust.
- **rq-0-17 array area.** It assumes 300–500 m². A 1–2.5 MWe array is roughly 6–40× larger. Flexible-body coupling during proximity operations is a first-order issue, not a detail.
- **rq-0-19 fleet result.** Its "15×150 t optimal" is a model-generated simulation output. It is not evidence and carries no TRL weight.

## 1. Evidence

All of the heritage below is at smaller mass. The ratios compare the 200–450 t stack with the active vehicle that flew.

| # | Heritage | Year | Demonstrated | Ratio | Confident |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Progress/Soyuz Kurs automated docking | 1980s–present | ~7 t active vehicle, hundreds of dockings in LEO | ~30–65× | Yes |
| 2 | ESA ATV automated docking to ISS | 2008–2014, 5 flights | ~20 t, fully automated GNC with optical/lidar relative navigation | ~10–22× | Yes |
| 3 | Shuttle docking to Mir and ISS (APAS) | 1995–2011 | ~100–120 t orbiter, crew-piloted. Closing rate ~0.03 m/s (approximate). | ~2–4× by mass; momentum to attenuate ~3–5×. Not autonomous; LEO. | Yes (masses approximate) |
| 4 | Canadarm2/SSRMS free-flyer capture and berthing of HTV, Dragon, Cygnus | 2009–present | ≤~16.5 t captured | ~12–27× | Yes |
| 4a | SSRMS published payload rating | — | ~116 t | Design rating only; never exercised in free-flyer capture | Somewhat |
| 5 | Crew Dragon autonomous docking (IDSS/NDS) | 2019– | ~12 t | ~17–37× | Yes |
| 6 | DARPA Orbital Express autonomous rendezvous and robotic capture | 2007 | ~1 t class | ~200–450× | Yes |
| 7 | Northrop Grumman MEV-1 (Intelsat 901, 2020) and MEV-2 (2021) | 2020–2021 | Docking to clients with no docking aids, GEO region, ~2–5 t bodies | ~50–200× | Yes on events; masses approximate |
| 8 | JAXA Hayabusa2 at Ryugu | 2018–2019 | ~0.6 t. Autonomous low-g touchdowns with target markers. Ion-engine rendezvous. Evasive retreat behind the asteroid during the SCI impact ejecta event. | ~300–700× | Yes |
| 9 | OSIRIS-REx at Bennu | 2018–2021 | ~2 t. Autonomous Natural Feature Tracking TAG (Oct 2020). ~1 km orbits. Ops continued through natural particle ejection (Lauretta et al., *Science*, 2019). | ~100–200× | Yes |
| 10 | Dawn EP rendezvous and orbit at Vesta and Ceres | 2007–2018 | ~1.2 t. Low-thrust approach to small bodies. | ~170–400× by mass; ~100× by power | Yes |
| 11 | SEL1 halo stationkeeping: ISEE-3 (1978), SOHO (1995–), ACE (1997–), DSCOVR (2015–) | 1978– | Single spacecraft, low annual Δv | No rendezvous or proximity operation has ever been flown at SEL1, to my knowledge | Yes |
| 12 | ISS attitude control with large flexible arrays | 1998– | ~100 kW-class, total array area ~2,500–3,000 m² (figure uncertain) | Area ~1–5×; never the active vehicle in proximity operations | Yes in general; area figure unsure |
| 13 | ESA PROBA-3 precision formation flying | Launched Dec 2024 | Two spacecraft, mm-class relative control | Small; HEO, not SEL1 | No (results status uncertain) |

### What has never been demonstrated, at any TRL

- Autonomous capture of a body above ~20 t.
- Any rendezvous at a Lagrange point.
- Proximity operations by a vehicle carrying MW-class flexible arrays.
- Proximity operations by a vehicle whose only main propulsion is ~10⁻⁴ m/s² EP.
- Navigation within an artificial, continuously generated debris environment, such as a mining site producing 13–47 kt/yr of tailings.

### Not evidence

- Gateway/NRHO rendezvous planning. It has not flown.
- The rq-0-17 and rq-0-19 trade discussions. These are design-study material.

## 2. Current TRL: 2–3

**Lower bound, TRL 2.** The exit criterion is met, though thinly. The concept and its benefit are documented in the round-2 architecture and rq-0-17: autonomous docking, berthing backup, or a dedicated handling craft. Node structure, orbit and traffic remain TBD.

**Upper bound, TRL 3.** I allow this only if the assessor accepts that heritage-validated models already cover the key parameters at scale. Those models are APAS/NDS contact dynamics, ATV/Dragon GNC and small-body navigation, all of whose flight data agreed with prediction. That is a defensible but generous reading.

**Unmet for TRL 3.** No project document gives analytical or experimental results validating predictions of the key parameters at stack scale:
- capture envelope;
- contact momentum and loads;
- passive-safety and abort Δv under ~10⁻⁴ m/s² authority;
- array–controller interaction;
- proximity-operations propellant;
- collision probability in the site debris field.

**Blocked for TRL 4.** The exit criterion requires a documented definition of the relevant environment. That cannot exist while node structure, traffic rate, SEL1 orbit family and the site debris environment are undefined. The debris environment depends on D-03.

### Sub-function view

The range above is for the integrated capability. Individual sub-functions sit at different levels, and this is why ratings will diverge.

| Sub-function | My estimate | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Relative-navigation sensors and algorithms | 5–6 | TRL 9 at heritage scale; an environment and range change only |
| SEL1 halo stationkeeping | 6 | Heritage at single-spacecraft scale; instability on a timescale of weeks, which is manageable |
| Low-thrust hovering near a small body | 5 | Dawn, Hayabusa2 |
| Contact, capture and mate of 150–300 t payloads | 2–3 | No autonomous capture above ~20 t |
| Flexible MW-array proximity GNC | 2–3 | Never flown as an active proximity vehicle |
| Collision avoidance in mining debris | 2 | The environment itself is unmodelled |

## 3. Target and difficulty

**Is it project-ending?** I classify T25 as architecture-change, not project-ending, because delivery can be redesigned around it (see §5). Under D-02 that gives:

| Milestone | Target TRL | What it requires |
|---|---|---|
| 0A mid-term review | 3, plus a documented relevant-environment definition | Analysis and simulation complete; environment written down |
| KDP-0B | 5 | The tug design and interface standard are frozen here. Assumed date ~2031–2034, my assumption; KDP-0B is unscheduled. |
| Tug CDR | 6 | Before the first operational arrival, which is 1.5–5 yr after first launch |

If the panel removes all fallbacks (a payload-transfer-only architecture), T25 becomes project-ending and the KDP-0B target rises to TRL 6 with no waivers.

**AD² = 5** for the step from 2–3 to 5. Similar developments have been done: autonomous docking, ~100 t piloted docking, autonomous small-body operations. The combination required here has not: autonomous, low-thrust, MW flexible arrays, 200–450 t, deep-space latency and self-generated debris. The path is nonetheless clear:

1. scaling analysis;
2. heritage-calibrated contact models;
3. hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) tests;
4. small-mass flight demonstration on 0A assets.

Sub-element difficulty varies:

| Sub-element | AD² | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| SEL1 operations | 3 | Well within the experience base |
| Contact at mass | 4–5 | Similar work done at lower mass |
| Flexible-array GNC | 5 | Not done at this scale |
| Debris avoidance | 5–6 | Rises to 6 if D-03 leaves the debris source term uncharacterised |

**Interface with D-05 (propellant selection).** Proximity abort cannot rely on the EP main engines. A secondary RCS is needed.
- Iodine cannot double as cold gas.
- Argon could act as a common-propellant cold-gas RCS at low Isp (~50 s, approximate).
- This should be fed into D-05.

## 4. Path

| # | Step | Method | Scale | Cost (USD) | Duration | Reaches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Relevant-environment and requirements definition: node structure, SEL1 orbit family (amplitude sized to avoid solar-exclusion comms outages and to coordinate with SOHO, ACE, DSCOVR and Aditya-L1), traffic, stack mass/inertia/array modes, debris source term from the D-03 tailings model | Analysis | Full architecture | 0.5–2 M | 0.5–1 yr | Prerequisite for the TRL 4 exit |
| 2 | Heritage data mining: ATV, HTV and Dragon approach/capture statistics; Shuttle APAS contact data; Hayabusa2 and OSIRIS-REx proximity logs; MEV docking data | Literature | Heritage set | 0.2–0.6 M | 0.5 yr | Supports TRL 3 |
| 3 | 6-DOF multibody simulation: tug, flexible arrays, payload and node. Contact models calibrated on step-2 data. Monte Carlo of capture envelope, loads, abort Δv, passive-safety trajectories, RCS sizing and debris conjunction rates. | Simulation | Full scale, 200–450 t | 2–6 M | 1–2 yr | 3 |
| 4 | HIL contact and GNC tests. Dynamically scaled capture mechanism on an air-bearing floor and a 6-DOF robotic facility (e.g. DLR EPOS, existence confident), with hybrid simulation of array flexibility. | Experiment | Scaled mechanism; full-scale software | 5–15 M | 1.5–3 yr | 4 |
| 5 | 0A flight experiments on scouts and pathfinder: autonomous low-thrust proximity ops and debris avoidance at the target NEA; release and recapture of a dummy container, or scout-to-scout rendezvous, at SEL1 | Experiment | 200–600 kg; ~500–2,000× below stack mass | 30–150 M incremental | 3–6 yr | 5, with documented scaling requirements |
| 6 | Subsystem prototype demonstration: a ~10–30 t stack with a large flexible array captures a dummy container at SEL1 or in high orbit, under dynamic-similarity scaling | Experiment | Still ~10–20× below required mass | 200–600 M | 4–7 yr | 6 |

Step 6 is a post-KDP-0B cost.

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk class: architecture-change.** Failing to reach target does not stop delivery, but it reshapes the delivery chain. The fallbacks, in order of preference:

1. **Integral payload.** The product stays on the tug's hardpoints. The node holds no mated hand-off; it accepts slow robotic offload or parks the whole tug-plus-payload.
2. **Small containers.** Use ~10–30 t containers handled by heritage-class mechanisms. This multiplies transfer count by ~5–30×, but at ~2–17 arrivals/yr the traffic is tolerable.
3. **Dedicated handling craft.** Gemini's option of a dedicated cargo-handling spacecraft at the node.
4. **No node.** Drop the SEL1 node and deliver directly to the Phase 1 consumer.

The most severe credible failure is a 300 t mis-capture at the node, which risks the tug (stated in rq-0-17 at $150–250M each) and the node. This argues for a passive-safe approach design whatever the TRL.

## 6. Where others might disagree

- **"It is all TRL 9 heritage, so rate it 4–6."** The strongest counter-case. Every sub-function has flown and ~100 t docking exists. My objection: that 100 t docking was crew-piloted in LEO, and the integration of autonomy, low thrust, MW flexible arrays, 200–450 t mass and a self-made debris field is unvalidated. Requirements are also undefined, so the TRL 4 exit is formally unmet.
- **Project-ending versus architecture-change.** If the panel treats payload transfer as essential to 0B economics, the target becomes TRL 6 at KDP-0B. That would likely force the step-6 demonstration before KDP-0B and add several years.
- **Scope.** If the architecture adopts integral-payload delivery, contact dynamics leaves T25. The remaining function (navigation, hovering, stationkeeping) rates ~4–5 today.
- **Debris avoidance.** Whether this is a T25 GNC problem or a D-03 licensing and environment problem. Its TRL cannot rise until the escaped-mass source term is characterised.
- **Assumed stack mass.** If tug dry mass is much higher than my 10–75 t estimate, all ratios worsen.

## Gemini 3.1 Pro


### 1. Evidence

Autonomous rendezvous, proximity operations, and docking (RPOD) are well-established in LEO and GEO, but the required scale (150–300 t payloads, likely 200–400 t total vehicle mass) and environments (SEL1, target NEA) present novel challenges in contact dynamics, plume impingement, and low-gravity stationkeeping.

- **ISS Resupply (ATV, Dragon, Cygnus, Progress):** Autonomous docking and berthing in LEO with vehicle masses up to ~20 t (ATV). Scale ratio: ~10–20× mass. Environment: LEO (not SEL1/NEA). Confident: true.
- **Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV-1/2, 2020/2021):** Autonomous rendezvous and docking in GEO. Mass: ~2.3 t. Scale ratio: ~100×. Confident: true.
- **DART (2022) / OSIRIS-REx (2020):** Autonomous terminal navigation to a NEA (DART) and touch-and-go sampling (OSIRIS-REx). Scale ratio: ~100× mass. Confident: true.

### 2. Current TRL

**TRL 3–4**
While the basic principles and algorithms of autonomous RPOD are TRL 9 for 20 t vehicles in Earth orbit, the specific application to 150–300 t payloads in SEL1 and NEA environments lacks component/breadboard validation of the contact dynamics and control systems at scale. The lower bound (TRL 3) reflects that analytical proof-of-concept for the required mass scale and multi-vehicle traffic management at SEL1/NEA exists in studies, but the upper bound (TRL 4) is not fully met because laboratory validation of the specific contact dynamics and high-inertia control algorithms has not been documented.

### 3. Target and difficulty

**Target:** TRL 6 by KDP-0B (project-ending for Phase 0B, as failure to safely dock and transfer cargo precludes the logistics chain).
**AD²: 4** (New development; similar development has been done). The algorithms and sensors exist, but scaling the contact dynamics, structural load management, and collision avoidance for 300 t vehicles requires significant engineering.

### 4. Path

1. **High-Fidelity Simulation:** 6-DOF simulation of contact dynamics, plume impingement, and control authority for 300 t vehicles at SEL1 and NEA. (Simulation, $1M–$3M, 1–2 years, reaches TRL 4).
2. **Hardware-in-the-Loop (HWIL) Testing:** Flat-floor or robotic testbed validation of docking sensors, algorithms, and scaled contact mechanisms. (Experiment, $5M–$15M, 2–3 years, reaches TRL 5).
3. **Subscale Space Demonstration:** Pathfinder mission (Phase 0A) demonstrating autonomous RPOD at the target NEA or SEL1 with a smaller vehicle, validating the environment and algorithms. (Experiment, $50M–$150M, 3–5 years, reaches TRL 6).

### 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk if fail:** Project-ending. If 300 t tugs cannot safely navigate and dock, the logistics architecture fails.
**Fallback:** Revert to smaller, heritage-scale cargo vehicles (e.g., 20 t), drastically increasing the fleet size and operational complexity (architecture-change).

### 6. Where others might disagree

Some might argue that RPOD is entirely software and sensor-driven, and therefore TRL 9 based on ISS heritage. However, the physical realities of arresting a 300 t mass without damaging the node or entangling large solar arrays make this a coupled cyber-physical problem that has not been validated at this scale.

## GPT-6.1 Sol


## T25 — Target-local and SEL1 cargo-node navigation and control

**Assessment: current TRL 2–3 for the architecture-specific integrated capability; target TRL 6 at KDP-0B; AD² 6.**

Individual capabilities have substantial flight heritage: autonomous rendezvous, asteroid-relative navigation, docking, and Sun–Earth L1 stationkeeping. **Their combination for repeated operations with 150–300 t payloads, large flexible electric-propulsion tugs, and an unspecified cargo node has not been demonstrated.** Heritage subsystem TRLs should not be transferred to this integrated capability.

### Assessment assumptions

- “SEL1” means **Sun–Earth L1**, with a controlled halo or Lissajous orbit—not a spacecraft held motionless at the mathematical equilibrium point.
- Target-local operations occur near an NEA, including a processing installation and possible dust, debris, irregular gravity and rotating structures.
- The assessed capability includes relative navigation, approach/departure guidance, collision avoidance, stationkeeping, capture/contact control and safe abort. It does **not** qualify the tug propulsion system or cargo handling hardware independently.
- Payload is 150–300 t; approaching vehicle mass is necessarily higher. Node mass, inertia, structural modes, interface design and total tug mass remain unknown.
- Repeated service is required, but the revised architecture does not specify a navigation-system lifetime or docking-cycle qualification requirement. The older 15-year requirement is treated as **provisional**, not adopted automatically.
- No calendar date for KDP-0B is supplied. Dates below are therefore milestone-relative.

Metallurgy-route selection matters only insofar as it changes the target installation’s rotation, geometry, plume/debris environment and docking interface. The three metallurgy routes do not warrant separate T25 ratings before those interfaces are defined.

## 1. Evidence

The ratios below compare **required payload mass alone** with demonstrated spacecraft mass. They are conservative indicators of a scaling gap—not complete dynamic similarity measures.

| Heritage | Demonstrated scale and environment | Required ÷ demonstrated | What it supports—and does not |
|---|---|---:|---|
| **ESA ATV Jules Verne, 2008** | Approximately 20.7 t vehicle; autonomous rendezvous and docking with ISS in LEO. The ATV programme completed five cargo missions, 2008–2015. | **7.2–14.5×**, before adding tug dry mass and propellant | Strong evidence for cooperative navigation, approach control, docking and repeated programme operations. Does not demonstrate large flexible tug dynamics, NEA operations or SEL1 cargo traffic. |
| **DARPA/NASA Orbital Express, 2007** | Two roughly tonne-class-or-smaller spacecraft demonstrated autonomous rendezvous, capture/docking and servicing in LEO. | **Order 150–300×** against a rounded 1 t scale; exact ratio depends on which body is compared | Supports autonomous servicing sequences and relative operations. It is not evidence for comparable capture inertia or industrial traffic. |
| **NASA OSIRIS-REx, 2020 TAG operation** | Natural Feature Tracking supported autonomous descent to Bennu and a brief sampling contact in the actual small-body environment. Launch mass was about 2.1 t; encounter mass was lower. | **At least 71–143×** using launch mass | Supports terrain-relative navigation and autonomous execution under communications delay. The compliant sampler contact was not cargo docking, and was not repeated production service. |
| **ESA/NASA SOHO, launched 1995; L1 operations from 1996 onward** | Approximately 1.85 t launch mass; long-duration Sun–Earth L1 halo-orbit operations and stationkeeping. | **At least 81–162×** using launch mass | Demonstrates the operational reality of L1 orbit determination and stationkeeping over decades. Does not demonstrate relative navigation, capture or collision avoidance at an L1 logistics node. |

**Sources:** ESA ATV/Jules Verne mission and programme documentation, 2008–2015; NASA/DARPA Orbital Express mission documentation, 2007; NASA OSIRIS-REx TAG and Natural Feature Tracking documentation, 2020; ESA/NASA SOHO mission documentation, 1995–present. I am confident these programmes and demonstrations exist. The Orbital Express mass comparison is deliberately approximate; it should be replaced by configuration-specific masses in the formal evidence dossier.

**Important scaling distinction:** mass alone does not necessarily make optical navigation harder. It does change available acceleration, stopping distance, angular momentum, collision consequence and contact dynamics. Moment-of-inertia and structural-mode ratios cannot be calculated until tug and node geometry are specified.

No cited programme demonstrates the required integrated T25 capability.

## 2. Current TRL and unmet exit criteria

### Integrated rating: **TRL 2–3**

- **Lower bound, TRL 2:** the application is formulated, with identifiable functions and established physical principles. Feasibility benefits from demonstrated constituent technologies.
- **Upper bound, TRL 3:** defensible only where documented heritage test/flight results validate critical functions that remain applicable to the proposed design. This is strongest for relative-navigation principles and L1 orbit control—not for the complete arrival/contact/transfer/departure sequence.

**Conservative KDP bookkeeping should use TRL 2 until an architecture-specific evidence dossier establishes the TRL 3 mapping.** None of the supplied consensus statements or logistics simulations provides that mapping.

**Next unmet criterion:**
- From TRL 2: documented analytical or experimental validation of **architecture-specific key parameters**, using test data.
- From a defensible TRL 3: an integrated breadboard with documented performance agreeing with predictions, plus a documented relevant environment, is needed for **TRL 4**.

The unresolved node, orbit and traffic definition also prevents a sound TRL 5 scaling assessment.

### Traffic must be reconciled before qualification

The revised fleet implies approximately:

\[
10/5 \ \text{to}\ 18/1.5 = 2–12
\]

loaded arrivals per year, assuming one delivered payload per round trip and full fleet availability.

The product requirement separately implies:

\[
600/300 \ \text{to}\ 2500/150 = 2–16.7
\]

loaded arrivals per year.

These envelopes are not jointly achievable at every combination of assumptions. Neither specifies peak simultaneous occupancy, holding queues or abort conflicts. **Peak traffic, not annual average alone, must set collision-avoidance requirements.**

The older claim that increasing handling time from 24 to 48 hours “halves fleet capacity” is not generally valid for 1.5–5-year round trips; berth bottlenecks would have to be demonstrated.

## 3. Target and difficulty

| Milestone | Target | Required evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Internal 0A review | **TRL 4** | Integrated laboratory demonstration with sensor, actuator and contact-dynamics test data |
| Later internal 0A milestone | **TRL 5** | Breadboard validation in defined relevant conditions, with documented scaling requirements |
| **KDP-0B, before authorising dependent production capability** | **TRL 6** | Integrated subsystem prototype demonstration in a relevant environment, with results agreeing with predictions |

**AD²: 6 — competing approaches remain, and the development path is not yet selected.**

The uncertainty is principally engineering and architecture integration, not unknown fundamental science:

- Direct docking versus robotic berthing versus free-flying cargo handling;
- Rigid versus compliant capture and allowable approach speed;
- Coupled tug/node flexible dynamics;
- Safe retreat authority when main electric propulsion is unsuitable for terminal manoeuvres;
- Fault containment without prompt ground intervention;
- Rotation and debris exclusion near the target plant.

A frozen cooperative node with passive targets, separated approach lanes and conventional capture could reduce AD² toward **5**. A rotating, debris-exposed interface or novel non-contact capture could increase it toward **7**.

**Estimated development time:** **5–9 years from funded start**, conditional on interface freeze and flight-demonstrator access. This is a planning estimate, not a committed schedule.

## 4. Path to TRL 6

Costs are **rough-order-of-magnitude development estimates**, not quotations. They exclude production tugs, the production cargo node and a complete mining/processing installation.

| Step | Scale and method | Cost | Duration | TRL consequence |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Define envelope and correlate models** | Literature audit, heritage-data review and test-correlated analysis covering 150–300 t payloads, total mass/inertia bounds, both operational sites and peak traffic | **$2–6M** | **0.5–1 yr** | Establishes architecture-specific **TRL 3**, only if predictions are validated against suitable physical data |
| **Integrated navigation/control breadboard** | Real flight-like sensors, processors and actuator interfaces; optical scene generation; six-degree-of-freedom hardware-in-the-loop; robot/air-bearing contact tests | **$10–30M** | **1–2 yr** | **TRL 4** |
| **Relevant-environment component and scaling campaign** | Thermal-vacuum sensor/interface tests; radiation qualification work; dust/illumination testing where applicable; flexible-structure and capture tests spanning predicted modal and impedance ranges | **$20–60M** | **1.5–3 yr** | **TRL 5**, if relevant conditions and scaling requirements are documented |
| **Integrated space prototype plus full-scale correlation** | Repeated autonomous approaches, capture, departure and injected-fault aborts with a roughly **10–30 t approaching vehicle** and cooperative target; full-scale interface tests and validated models covering the required mass/inertia envelope | **$150–450M** | **3–5 yr**, partly overlapping | **Potential TRL 6**, subject to demonstrated similarity and predictive agreement |

### Conditions on the final step

A 10–30 t flight vehicle leaves a **5–30× payload-mass gap**. A space demonstration does not erase that gap merely by flying.

The evidence must cover:

- Effective contact mass, interface stiffness/damping and structural modes;
- Sensor performance under NEA-like lighting and target geometry;
- Terminal manoeuvre authority, actuator faults and plume constraints;
- Loss of navigation, communications and power during close approach;
- Concurrent departure/arrival conflicts and safe holding;
- Capture/latch wear over the required service cycles;
- Node attitude disturbances and recovery after transfer.

Reduced-scale flight evidence must be tied to full-scale physical tests and validated extrapolation. If that cannot be defended, the demonstrator must become larger or the architecture must change.

A LEO demonstration alone does not reproduce NEA gravity, dust or the SEL1 operational geometry. The test programme must establish which environmental differences matter and demonstrate the affected functions separately. **TRL 6 is a conditional outcome, not a guaranteed reward for completing the listed activities.**

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk class: architecture-change.**

Failure would prevent use of the reference docking/berthing architecture, but does not necessarily end all 0B options. Alternatives include:

- Smaller independently controlled cargo parcels;
- A stand-off depot with segregated transfer lanes;
- Dedicated handling craft;
- Capture at a non-rotating, isolated target-local interface.

These alternatives require their own qualification and may impose substantial cost or throughput penalties.

**If no alternative achieves TRL 6 by KDP-0B, dependent 0B production cannot pass D-02.** The fallback is 0A-only research with Earth-supplied Phase 1 material. In that circumstance, this technology becomes project-ending for the proposed 0B delivery architecture.

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **TRL 2–3 versus 4–5:** an assessor defining T25 narrowly as conventional cooperative rendezvous software could cite much higher heritage maturity. That excludes the coupled mass, flexible structures, contact and traffic functions explicitly required here.
2. **Mass as a scaling measure:** some navigation functions scale weakly with mass. Agreed; the low integrated rating is driven mainly by coupled control/contact dynamics and missing system definition.
3. **Whether space testing is necessary for TRL 6:** a sufficiently representative ground prototype can satisfy TRL 6 for some functions. Here, combined microgravity contact and flexible-body dynamics make space correlation valuable; it is not a universal NASA requirement.
4. **Direct docking versus berthing:** neither is selected by the evidence presented. Magnetic/electrostatic capture is an additional development option, not demonstrated heritage for this load class.
5. **Risk classification:** it becomes project-ending if demand, cost or schedule rules exclude smaller parcels and alternate transfer architectures. Those constraints have not yet been established.

# T25 consolidated rating: target-local and SEL1 cargo-node navigation and control

## 1. Ratings by model

| | Claude Opus 5.5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Current TRL** | 2–3 | 3–4 | 2–3 (use TRL 2 for KDP bookkeeping until an evidence dossier exists) |
| **AD²** | 5 (sub-elements 3 to 5–6) | 4 | 6 (5 if interfaces freeze, 7 if rotating or novel capture) |
| **Target at KDP-0B** | TRL 5 | TRL 6 | TRL 6 |
| **Other milestones** | TRL 3 plus environment definition at 0A mid-term; TRL 6 by tug CDR | None stated | TRL 4 at internal 0A review; TRL 5 at a later 0A milestone |
| **Risk class** | Architecture-change. Becomes project-ending, with TRL 6 required at KDP-0B, if all fallbacks are removed. | Project-ending. Its own fallback is labelled architecture-change. | Architecture-change. Becomes project-ending if no alternative reaches TRL 6 by KDP-0B. |
| **Years to target** | 4–8 (to TRL 5) | 4–7 (to TRL 6) | 5–9 (to TRL 6, from funded start) |
| **Phase need** | 0B | 0B | 0B |
| **Confidence** | Medium | Medium | Medium |

The year figures refer to different target TRLs, so they cannot be compared directly.

## 2. Where the models agree

- **Constituent functions are mature; the integrated capability is not.** All three say relative-navigation sensors, autonomous docking and small-body or L1 operations have flight heritage. All three say the integrated function at 150–300 t payload scale has never been demonstrated. All three reject transferring heritage TRL 9 to T25 and name this as the main counter-argument.
- **The gap is physical, not software.** Contact dynamics, high inertia, and interaction with large flexible arrays are the drivers. GPT adds that some navigation functions scale only weakly with mass.
- **No heritage autonomous capture comes near the required mass.** All three cite the ~20 t ATV-class vehicle as the largest relevant autonomous docker.
- **The path has the same shape in all three:**
  1. analysis and 6-DOF simulation;
  2. hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) or air-bearing/robotic contact testing;
  3. flight demonstration at reduced scale.

  The 6-DOF simulation and HIL steps have broadly overlapping cost bands.
- **Fallback:** all three name smaller cargo units (~10–30 t containers or parcels) as a fallback. Claude and GPT also name dedicated handling craft and stand-off or alternative transfer architectures.
- **Definition gaps:** Claude and GPT both state that node structure, orbit and traffic are undefined. Both treat this as blocking the TRL 4 exit (Claude) or a sound TRL 5 scaling assessment (GPT).

## 3. Where they diverge, and why

### 3.1 Current TRL: 3–4 (Gemini) versus 2–3 (Claude, GPT)

- **Gemini's position.** It sets the lower bound at TRL 3 because "analytical proof-of-concept for the required mass scale … exists in studies". No study is named.
- **Claude's position.** No project document gives analytical or experimental results validating the key parameters at stack scale (capture envelope, contact loads, abort Δv, array–controller interaction, debris collision probability). It explicitly excludes the rq-0-17 and rq-0-19 trade discussions as evidence.
- **GPT's position.** It reaches the same conclusion: none of the supplied consensus statements or logistics simulations provides the architecture-specific TRL 3 mapping.
- **What would settle it.** Produce and review the studies Gemini refers to, or an architecture-specific evidence dossier mapping heritage results to these parameters. GPT's step 1 and Claude's steps 2–3 are designed to create that dossier.

### 3.2 KDP-0B target: TRL 5 (Claude) versus TRL 6 (Gemini, GPT)

- **Claude** reads KDP-0B as the tug design and interface freeze, with an assumed date of ~2031–2034. It places TRL 6 at tug CDR. This follows from its architecture-change classification under D-02.
- **GPT** reads KDP-0B as the gate before authorising dependent production, which in its reading requires TRL 6.
- **Gemini** derives TRL 6 from its project-ending classification.
- **What would settle it.** This is a definitional and panel question, not an evidence question. It needs:
  - a ruling on what KDP-0B gates;
  - a KDP-0B date, which none of the models had;
  - a ruling on the risk class (§3.3).

### 3.3 Risk class

- **Gemini** classifies T25 as project-ending. Its fallback (reverting to ~20 t vehicles with a larger fleet) is itself labelled architecture-change, which is internally inconsistent.
- **Claude and GPT** classify it as architecture-change, with conditions under which it becomes project-ending:
  - Claude: if payload transfer is essential to 0B economics.
  - GPT: if demand, cost or schedule rules exclude smaller parcels and alternative transfer.
- **What would settle it.** A cost and throughput assessment of the fallbacks (integral payload, small containers, handling craft, no node) against 0B economics.

### 3.4 AD²: 4, 5 or 6

- **Gemini (4):** similar development has been done.
- **Claude (5):** the path is clear even though the combination is new. It splits the rating by sub-element: SEL1 operations 3, contact at mass 4–5, flexible-array GNC 5, debris avoidance 5–6.
- **GPT (6):** competing approaches remain unselected (direct docking, robotic berthing, free-flying handler; rigid versus compliant capture).
- **What would settle it.** Selection of the capture and transfer concept and an interface freeze. GPT itself says a frozen cooperative node would move its rating toward 5.

### 3.5 Can a 200–600 kg 0A demonstrator reach TRL 6?

- **Gemini** says the 0A pathfinder demonstration reaches TRL 6.
- **Claude** says 0A flights reach TRL 5 only, with documented scaling requirements. TRL 6 needs a ~10–30 t stack with a large flexible array, which it places after KDP-0B.
- **GPT** also requires a ~10–30 t vehicle for TRL 6, placed before KDP-0B. It warns that even this leaves a 5–30× payload-mass gap, which must be closed by full-scale interface tests and validated extrapolation.
- **Cost consequence.** The arithmetic sums of each model's stated step costs are:

  | Model | Sum of step costs | Note |
  |---|---|---|
  | Gemini | ~$56–168M | Path ends at TRL 6 |
  | GPT | ~$182–546M | Path ends at TRL 6 |
  | Claude | ~$238–774M | Last step is post-KDP-0B |

  These are simple sums of the stated ranges. Durations overlap and phasing differs between models.
- **What would settle it.** A documented dynamic-similarity and scaling analysis showing whether a subscale flight is representative for contact, inertia and flexible modes. This is the output of Claude's 6-DOF Monte Carlo step and GPT's envelope-and-correlation step.

### 3.6 Scale basis for ratios

The models divide by different masses, so their scale ratios are not directly comparable:
- **Claude** uses its own estimate of total stack mass, ~200–450 t. It derives this from an assumed tug dry mass of 10–75 t and flags it as not project data.
- **Gemini** assumes a total of ~200–400 t.
- **GPT** uses payload mass only. It states that total mass and inertia ratios are higher or TBD and cannot be computed until tug and node geometry exist.

**What would settle it:** project tug mass, power and array geometry data.

### 3.7 Single-model analytical claims (not cross-checked by the other models)

| Claim | Model |
|---|---|
| rq-0-17 overstates sustained acceleration by 15–1,500× (it uses 0.01–0.1 m/s² against ~10⁻⁴ derived), so design-driving loads are contact and RCS transients, not thrust | Claude |
| rq-0-17 array area of 300–500 m² is ~6–40× too small | Claude |
| The rq-0-19 "15×150 t optimal" result carries no TRL weight | Claude |
| Debris is the weakest sub-function (collision avoidance in mining debris, TRL 2), tied to the D-03 tailings source term | Claude |
| Proximity abort cannot use the EP main engines, so a secondary RCS is needed; argon could serve as a common-propellant cold-gas RCS at ~50 s Isp (approximate), iodine could not. Proposed as a D-05 input. | Claude |
| Fleet-derived traffic (2–12 arrivals/yr) and product-derived traffic (2–16.7/yr) are not jointly achievable at every combination; peak occupancy, not the annual average, should set collision-avoidance requirements | GPT |
| The earlier claim that 24→48 h handling time "halves fleet capacity" is not generally valid for 1.5–5 yr round trips | GPT |
| A representative ground prototype can satisfy TRL 6 for some functions; space testing is not a universal NASA requirement | GPT |
| Plume impingement is a scaling issue | Gemini |

Claude also gives a single traffic range of ~2–17 arrivals/yr, which it does not test for joint feasibility as GPT does.

**What would settle these:**
- independent re-derivation of the rq-0-17 acceleration and area figures from stated power and Isp;
- reconciliation of the traffic numbers by the rq-0-19/rq-0-20 owners;
- the D-03 debris source term.

### 3.8 Scope boundary

- **Claude** excludes NEA surface lift and the EP propulsion string. It notes that if integral-payload delivery is adopted, contact dynamics leaves T25 and the remaining navigation, hovering and stationkeeping function rates ~4–5.
- **GPT** excludes independent qualification of the propulsion system and of cargo-handling hardware.
- **Gemini** states no explicit scope boundary.
- **Debris:** Claude raises, without resolving, whether debris avoidance belongs to T25 or to D-03.

These boundaries are for the panel to set.

## 4. Evidence

| Citation | Cited by | Notes and flags |
|---|---|---|
| ESA ATV automated docking, ~20 t, 5 flights | All three | Programme end date differs: Claude 2008–2014, GPT 2008–2015. GPT gives 20.7 t. Ratios differ because of the denominator: Claude 10–22× (stack), GPT 7.2–14.5× (payload), Gemini 10–20×. |
| OSIRIS-REx autonomous NFT-guided TAG at Bennu, 2020 | All three | GPT notes the sampling contact was compliant and brief, not docking. Claude adds operations continued through natural particle ejection, citing Lauretta et al., *Science*, 2019 (Claude only). |
| Orbital Express, 2007, ~1 t class | Claude, GPT | GPT marks its mass comparison as deliberately approximate. |
| MEV-1/MEV-2 docking without docking aids, GEO | Claude, Gemini | Claude gives ~2–5 t (masses approximate); Gemini gives ~2.3 t. |
| SEL1 halo stationkeeping | Claude (ISEE-3, SOHO, ACE, DSCOVR), GPT (SOHO, ~1.85 t) | Claude says no Lagrange-point rendezvous has been flown "to my knowledge". |
| Progress/Soyuz Kurs, Crew Dragon IDSS/NDS, Cygnus | Claude in detail; Gemini in a general list | |
| **Shuttle docking to Mir/ISS via APAS, ~100–120 t, crew-piloted** | **Claude only** | Masses and the ~0.03 m/s closing rate are marked approximate. This is the only heritage item within ~2–4× of the required mass, and it was not autonomous. |
| **Canadarm2/SSRMS capture of free-flyers ≤~16.5 t; ~116 t rating** | **Claude only** | The 116 t figure is marked "somewhat" confident and is a design rating, never exercised in free-flyer capture. |
| **Hayabusa2 at Ryugu** (autonomous touchdown, retreat during the SCI ejecta event) | **Claude only** | |
| **Dawn EP rendezvous at Vesta and Ceres** | **Claude only** | |
| **ISS attitude control with large flexible arrays** | **Claude only** | Array area figure (~2,500–3,000 m²) marked **unsure**. |
| **ESA PROBA-3 precision formation flying** | **Claude only** | Marked **not confident**; results status uncertain. |
| **DART terminal navigation to an NEA, 2022** | **Gemini only** | Gemini's prose groups it at ~100× mass; its YAML gives ~0.6 t and ~500×. The two figures are inconsistent. |
| DLR EPOS 6-DOF facility | Claude only | Cited as a test facility, not as evidence; existence marked confident. |

**Evidence the models reject:**
- **Claude:** Gateway/NRHO rendezvous planning (not flown), and the rq-0-17 and rq-0-19 trades.
- **GPT:** the supplied consensus statements and logistics simulations.
- **Gemini:** relies on unnamed "studies" for its TRL 3 floor; see §3.1.

**Strongest common evidence:** ATV at ~20 t and OSIRIS-REx small-body autonomy, both cited by all three. **Most scale-relevant single-model evidence:** Shuttle APAS at ~100–120 t, cited by Claude only, crew-piloted, with approximate masses. It should be independently verified before it carries weight.

## 5. Consolidated path

The steps below merge the models' sequences. Where a model has no equivalent step, it is marked "—". TRL reached is shown in brackets after each cost and duration.

| # | Step | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Relevant-environment and requirements definition:** node structure, SEL1 orbit family, peak and average traffic, stack mass/inertia/array modes, D-03 debris source term | $0.5–2M, 0.5–1 yr (prerequisite for TRL 4) | — | Folded into step 2 |
| 2 | **Heritage data mining and model correlation** | $0.2–0.6M, 0.5 yr (supports TRL 3) | — | $2–6M, 0.5–1 yr, combined with step 1 (TRL 3, only if predictions validate against physical data) |
| 3 | **6-DOF multibody / contact simulation and Monte Carlo** | $2–6M, 1–2 yr (3) | $1–3M, 1–2 yr (4) | Within step 2 |
| 4 | **HIL / air-bearing / robotic contact and GNC breadboard** | $5–15M, 1.5–3 yr (4) | $5–15M, 2–3 yr (5) | $10–30M, 1–2 yr (4) |
| 5 | **Relevant-environment component and scaling campaign:** thermal-vacuum, radiation, dust/illumination, flexible-mode and capture-impedance tests | — | — | $20–60M, 1.5–3 yr (5) |
| 6 | **0A flight experiments, 200–600 kg:** NEA low-thrust proximity and debris avoidance; SEL1 release/recapture or scout-to-scout rendezvous | $30–150M, 3–6 yr (5) | $50–150M, 3–5 yr (6) | Not a separate step |
| 7 | **~10–30 t integrated space prototype with large flexible array**, repeated captures and injected-fault aborts, plus full-scale correlation | $200–600M, 4–7 yr, post-KDP-0B, before tug CDR (6) | — | $150–450M, 3–5 yr, before KDP-0B; TRL 6 conditional on demonstrated similarity (6) |

**Fallbacks, combined across models:**
- integral payload with no mated hand-off (Claude);
- ~10–30 t containers or parcels (all three);
- dedicated node handling craft (Claude, GPT);
- stand-off depot with segregated lanes, or an isolated non-rotating interface (GPT);
- no SEL1 node, delivering direct to the consumer (Claude);
- 0A-only with Earth supply if no alternative reaches TRL 6 (GPT).

## 6. Decisions and inputs needed to close the divergences

1. **KDP-0B:** a definition (design freeze or production authorisation) and a date. This settles §3.2.
2. **Risk class:** a ruling informed by a fallback cost and throughput assessment. This settles §3.2 and §3.3.
3. **Evidence for a TRL 3 floor:** Gemini's referenced studies, or a commissioned architecture-specific evidence dossier. This settles §3.1.
4. **Scaling and similarity analysis:** shows whether 200–600 kg or 10–30 t flight evidence can support TRL 6. This settles §3.5 and the cost spread.
5. **Capture-concept selection and interface freeze.** This settles §3.4.
6. **Project data:** tug mass, power and array geometry; reconciled peak traffic; the D-03 debris source term; and independent re-derivation of the rq-0-17 acceleration and area figures. This settles §3.6 and §3.7.
7. **Scope and cross-references:** a panel ruling on T25 scope (integral payload, debris ownership), and whether to forward Claude's RCS-propellant point to D-05. This settles §3.7 and §3.8.
